semantics.note: Keeps the exceptions and the 'appears' qualifier. Saying 'in AI' is a little broader than the GPU-buyer context, but that doesn't change the result. 'Seems' qualifies the claim, but it isn't a probabilistic forecast hedge, so this stays a checkable observation.

contract.note: Reading 'make money' as net profit from generative AI, measured in the last reported quarter before publication, is an ordinary reading. The contract leaves the accounting basis open, which is fair. The result depends on the chosen period and profit measure.

evidence.note: Says Midjourney became profitable in 2022, with no measure given. That is a different period from the target quarter, so it cannot contradict the claim. It is only a candidate counterexample.
CoreWeave's filing shows a $291M net loss for Q2 2025. That is one company, and a single loss cannot establish that no generative AI business outside the exceptions was profitable.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs broad evidence that no generative AI business outside the exceptions made a profit in Q2 2025. The contradiction condition needs one business with a demonstrated target-period net profit. The packet has one loss-making compute provider and a 2022 Midjourney profitability statement. Neither settles the claim either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. Merchant is cited only in the surrounding text.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both halves: some AI job losses happened, and white-collar workers and software engineers were excluded. It drops 'or really any of the career paths', which is a minor omission.

contract.note: Zitron's own examples (translators, copy editors) are contractors, so reading 'white collar' as salaried office staff matches his distinction. The categorical sentence is firm. Treating confirmed AI-driven losses of salaried HR and support staff as contradiction is an ordinary reading, not a stretch, though the result depends on that reading.

evidence.note: An IBM employee-representative document from May 2024 says a Q1 2024 job cut was explicitly triggered by AI and automation, mostly in support functions, and that staff had already left. This is white-collar displacement before publication.

Reporting from May 2025 says IBM's CEO confirmed AI replaced hundreds of HR employees, with layoffs. This is a company statement about itself, but it is corroborated by e1. The loss is salaried white-collar and happened before publication.
SHRM notes IBM's net headcount rose. That limits any inference about net job loss, but the article still says particular HR workers were replaced.

reviews.rationale: The claim says salaried white-collar workers had not lost jobs to AI. Before September 2025, IBM's European works council recorded an AI- and automation-triggered job cut in support functions, and IBM's CEO confirmed hundreds of HR roles were replaced by AI. That meets the contradiction condition. Net hiring elsewhere (e3) doesn't undo these individual losses. The packet does not establish losses among software engineers.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Keeps the exclusion of OpenAI and Anthropic and the negative-margin claim. It drops the 'struggling to stay alive' and fundraising parts, but the core proposition is intact.

contract.note: Treating the sentence as a broad claim about the startup population, and counting free-user costs in gross margin as Zitron's context does, is fair. The quarter and the prevalence threshold come from the evaluator, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Replit's $250M raise in September 2025 matches the described fundraising pattern. It gives no margin or runway data, and it falls after the target quarter.

Published April 2026, before the evaluation date. It relays press estimates of a positive Lovable margin and Replit margins that varied in 2025. Cost definitions are unclear and the sample is not representative, so it can't contradict a population-wide claim.
Midjourney's founder said in 2022 that the company was profitable. That is a different period and gives no gross-margin figure.

reviews.rationale: Both conditions require representative, consistently measured margin and financial-health evidence for Q2 2025. The packet has one funding announcement, scattered press margin estimates (some positive) for two companies, and a 2022 profitability statement. None of this settles whether the startup population generally had negative gross margins and was in distress.

attribution.note: Zitron's own conditional calculation. The $50bn figure is attributed to others, but the inference is his.

semantics.note: Keeps the antecedent (the $50bn per GW figure is accurate) and the 10GW / $500bn / $100bn structure. Given the premise, the consequent is mostly arithmetic.

contract.note: Requiring the antecedent to be independently established and setting no deadline is faithful. Counting partner-financed spending matches Zitron's own context.

evidence.note: OpenAI's letter-of-intent announcement says Nvidia will invest progressively as each GW is deployed. It gives no realized construction costs.
Reuters relays Huang's estimate of about $50bn per GW. A prospective estimate doesn't establish the antecedent.

Huang said the agreement was finalized at $30B and called $100B unlikely. That is not a definitive end to the transaction, and the cost antecedent is still unestablished, so it can't resolve the claim early.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional with no deadline. No realized cost records establish the $50bn per GW antecedent, so the claim can't be scored. Huang's March 2026 remarks about a smaller $30B deal do not meet the early-resolution rule, which needs a definitive transaction-ending event and an established antecedent. No 10GW spending records exist yet.
